Having bowed her head, the goddess Gaurī questioned Śaṅkara.
O Lord, O Protector of the World, O Sovereign of the Universe, I wish to hear [this].
O Lord of Gods, grant me your grace; speak that which accomplishes the goals of dharma and artha.
Subjugation, eradication, delusion, as well as immobilization, pacification, and nourishment— these and many other such rites.

The illustrious Lord said:

I shall tell it all to you, O Goddess, as it has been fully proclaimed.

One shall slay the enemy by means of medicinal herbs and the recitation of mantras; of this there is no doubt. Having extracted the essence from the Uḍḍīśa, I have spoken this to you out of devotion. (8)
Having paid homage to Uḍḍīśa and to Rudra, who is indeed very difficult to attain—
the one with matted hair, the odd-eyed one, who removes the fear of all beings— 9.
I shall describe the yogas arising from Rudra, which destroy all enemies;
when these are employed, they instantly take away life—of this there is no doubt. (10)
The first is the act of bringing beings into existence, the second is intoxication,
the third is hatred, and the fourth is likewise eradication.
The fifth is the expulsion of a village, and the sixth is the immobilization of water;
then follows the quenching of fire, and the supreme art of subjugation.
Listen also, O fair-faced one, to many other applications;
these yogas were taught by Śiva in the Uḍḍīśa, the definitive scripture. (13)
It causes blindness, muteness, and deafness; likewise, it brings about the fever of elemental spirits and the neutralization of missiles and weapons. (14)
It pacifies the defects of water, destroys the potency of honey, causes the destruction of the senses of the intoxicated, and provokes elephants and horses. (15)
It certainly effects the summoning of serpents as well as men;
it brings about the destruction of fire and indeed the destruction of leaves. (16)
The making of oneself into a donkey, entering another's body,

And other numerous applications that are fierce and hair-raising,

What will he who does not know the Uḍḍīśa do when the [deity] is enraged? 19.
One might move Sumeru from its place, flood the earth with oceans, or cause the sun to fall to the ground; yet this [my word] shall not become false. (20)
Just as Indra has his thunderbolt and Varuṇa his noose,
as Yama has his staff and Kubera his mace; (21)
Just as the power of Agni has been described, and just as the sword belongs to Nirṛti,
so too is the goad of Vāyu, and the trident of the Trident-bearer.

so too have these great yogas been employed for the sake of the enemy.
Even when [the obstacle] has not yet ceased, they turn back; there is no doubt about this.

I shall describe the ritual for those engaged [in this practice], the supreme means for subduing enemies;
by the mere performance of which, a spirit seizes a human being. (25)
Taking a piece of neem wood measuring four finger-breadths in length,
one should smear it with the excrement of an enemy and likewise inscribe the name [thereon].
O Maheśvarī, one should offer incense made from the charcoal of a funeral pyre under that [same] name;
having stationed oneself within the cremation ground, one should take earth from the body of such a person.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
a spirit (bhūta) who has been consecrated with this mantra will quickly seize him. || 28 ||

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of all beings, Virūpākṣa, who is eternally fierce, fanged, and terrifying; together with the planets, yakṣas, bhūtas, and vetālas, O Śaṅkara, burn, burn the human being! Cook, cook! Seize, seize! Cause to be seized, cause to be seized! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
If one should desire to bring [the deity] back, this rite is performed for him:
one should cause the Lord Īśāna to be gratified with ghee and *vacā* grass. (29)
One should offer guggulu incense mixed with clarified butter on all sides;
having consecrated it with the mantra, health will indeed be restored.
The mantra: Oṃ, homage to Śiva, the peaceful, the radiant, the liberated, the god of gods, who possesses white arms; pacify, pacify the disease! May [Name] be well; homage be to you! Thus.
The Mantra for Health.
Now I shall further explain another practice that is difficult to find on earth;
by the mere performance of which, fever seizes a human being. (31)
Having fashioned a figure out of nimba wood measuring four finger-breadths in size, one should [place] poison, *unmatta*, black mustard seeds, and salt within its heart.

Then, within half a watch (prahara), he is seized by the fever-spirit.

By means of which mere knowledge the eradication of an enemy occurs:
[the use of] *brahmadaṇḍī*, funeral ashes, and likewise cow dung. (36)

Then, for the purpose of bringing him back [to health], one should bathe him with cow's milk;

By burying [the mantra] at the gate of an enemy, O Goddess of Gods, one shall swiftly drive away the foes; within seven nights, their entire household shall perish along with its very roots.
Now I shall describe the rite for inciting enmity against enemies; listen, O Śaṅkarī, by the mere performance of which hatred arises among men. (44)
Brahmadaṇḍī, together with its roots and combined with the flesh of a crow,
should be infused repeatedly for seven nights with the juice of Jātī flowers.
Then, one should infuse it with cat urine for seven days;
thereafter, this incense should be offered in the midst of the enemy's clan.

the wise practitioner, having taken liquor and human flesh, [should proceed]. (48)

within seven days, Māra shall be overcome, as spoken by Rudra. (49)
Brahmadaṇḍī, funeral ashes, liquor, and meat;
the leaves of ariṣṭa, poison, and blood as well. (50)
And it should be employed for the delusion of enemies through the application of the *nāma* [mantra];
by a seven-night practice, there is the destruction of all enemies. (51)
Having consecrated one hundred and eight [offerings] with the mantra, the wise one should present them to the enemy for these malevolent yogas. 52.

Having worshipped the Lord Īśāna, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.

it should also be employed against an enemy army by a king seeking victory. (54)

Then he should smear his limbs with [fragrant substances], or likewise with bones,

This great mantra is a remedy that strikes fear into malevolent spirits;
having consecrated food and drink with it, one should employ them according to the prescribed rite.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, to Rudra, the peaceful one, possessed of divine yoga, of divine form, the matted-haired celibate student, the one consecrated by the three worlds; O you of great power, hundred-fold, the essence of mind! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Svāhā!
Being afflicted, one should recite the mantra while remaining pure and composed;
then, one should recite this mantra one thousand and eight times.
One should grind it with a maiden with great effort in the middle of a cow-pen; if that is impossible, one should do so repeatedly according to one's ability upon a funeral pyre.
Spoken by Rudra himself, these accomplish all undertakings;
indeed, they should all be employed as destroyers of every enemy. (70)
Therefore, one who is diligent in practice should protect [the teachings] with every effort;
it must never be spoken to those who lack devotion, nor likewise to cruel or sinful people. (71)
"It should be given to one who is endowed with devotion and knowledgeable in the scriptures, O Mistress of the Immortals.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Uḍḍāmareśvara-mahātantra*, extracted from the *Vīrabhadreśvara-tantra* within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
The venerable Pārvatī said:
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for the immobilization of water:
[the use of] crocodiles, *velva* plants, fangs, blood, and even flesh. (1)
The heart of a tortoise and that of a porpoise,
one after another, should all be prepared together with the oil of the *vibhītaka* tree.
Then, having performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should remain comfortably in the water;
the essence of the Madraka, Lakṣaṇa, and Makara [fish] should be extracted.
One should take the head of a *ḍuṇḍubha* snake and cause all [the ingredients] to be prepared together;
furthermore, one should cause *vibhītaka* oil to be added while it is being cooked. (4)
One should perform the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*); [the oil] remains in the water for seven days.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, being composed, one should cook that oil in an iron vessel.
Having stayed for four months and worshipped the god Śaṅkara,
he performed the ritual bath with clay while consecrating it with a mantra as a sacrificial fee.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa);
having consecrated it with this [mantra], it then succeeds, and not otherwise.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara! Paralyze the water, paralyze it! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Now I shall describe the preparation of the spider-poison; listen to that in brief.
[Take] the juice of *bhallātaka*, *guñjā*, poison, and *citraka*. (8)
One should cause the hair of the *kapikacchapa* to be made into powder and administered;
this, combined with all [the aforementioned ingredients], is the supreme method for producing spiders.
I shall describe the form of that which is born with its characteristic marks:
the limbs emit smoke and faint repeatedly. (10)
Such would be the appearance of his symptoms caused by the spider;
I shall describe its treatment so that he may attain well-being. (11)
Uśīra, sandalwood, priyaṅgu, tagara,
red sandalwood, and kuṣṭha— this ointment destroys spiders.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara; O you who cause [the world] to sport, svāhā!
Having consecrated it with mantras, he will then become healthy.
One should take the head of a black cobra and place mustard seeds in its mouth. (13)
One should wrap it together with bhallātaka in a black thread and cook it inside a hollow of anthill clay over indirect smoke.
Having prepared a powder of *viṣa* combined with the hairs of the *kapikacchapa* in sixteen parts, one should cast it upon the heads of one's enemies.
The application of spider-silk [thread] is most excellent during the autumn, summer, and spring seasons;
then, when the body has been fomented, mustard seeds adhere to it. (16)
One should render even a spider venomous; there is no need for deliberation here. As soon as the pain arises, one should perform the recitation of the mantra as previously described.
By means of the previously described procedure, one becomes healthy as before. (p. 10) Now, I shall briefly describe the destruction of crops. || 18 ||
As soon as it is performed, the wise one, having fashioned a vajra, should cast it into whichever field he desires; therein the destruction of the crops occurs. (19)
The knower of mantras should cast [the oblation] there by means of the Māhendra application.
Now, I shall again declare the mantra that is to be employed in these applications. (20)
One should consecrate [the object] with this mantra exactly one hundred and eight times:
Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya vajraṃ vināśaya vajraṃ surapatirājñāpaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
One who applies this yoga through ritual action according to the prescribed rule shall cast away a leaf; by that very application of leaves, the [targeted] leaf perishes. || 21 ||
I shall speak again of eradication; listen, my son, exactly as it is, by the mere performance of which the eradication of a village occurs. (22)
Having taken earth from the four crossroads in the village, the wise man should fashion a figure with cow dung in the four directions of the village.
Having prepared the firewood for the funeral pyre with the feathers of cuckoos and crows,
and having offered a thousand oblations, one should then collect the ashes.
Having removed [the ashes] without distinction and formed a fist containing the ashes,
one should consecrate it with this very mantra recited one hundred times.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Mahākālarudra, the cause of the destruction of the three cities! Burn, burn! Blow, blow! Cook, cook! Grind, grind! Delude, delude! Intoxicate, intoxicate!
Annihilate, annihilate! The illustrious Mahārudra commands: [you] who produce sound, the Enchantress!
Bhagavati kheṃ kheṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Whether in a village or even in a city, by the scattering of ashes, the destruction of enemies occurs; of this there is no doubt. (26)
(11) Furthermore, the ashes are cast far away, and he dwells again in the city.
I shall explain the process of purification; listen to the yoga in brief. (27)

Furthermore, the wise one, having fashioned an image of the enemy in the form of a bull,
should consecrate it twenty-one times with this mantra.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara, the shatterer of desire! [Name], cchaḥ cchaḥ, svāhā!
And for those who have set out, the knower of mantras should perform the rite with this mantra.
Having prepared honey mixed with clarified butter, one should apply it to this spot;
then, having bathed with cow's milk, one will become healthy once more. (31)
Now, the procedure for causing madness: the root of *kanaka* seed, powdered with ghee, along with the droppings of a house sparrow and *karañja* seeds. (32)
This powder causes madness; by consuming it, one becomes insane.
It has been consecrated twenty-one times with this mantra. (33)

Cchaḥ cchaḥ svāhā!

Thus ends the procedure for causing intoxication.
Indeed, salt consecrated twenty-one times with this mantra becomes as harsh [as a donkey].

Food and drink, consecrated with this mantra one hundred times, should be given to any enemy whatsoever. (37)
And from eating [it], one shall become blind; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Oṃ, obeisance to Uḍḍāmareśvara! Render the body blind! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Svāhā!
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for causing leprosy.

the juice of *bhallātaka*, *guñjā*, and likewise *maṇḍalakārikā*. (39)

On the ninth day of these lunar dates, when conjoined with the asterisms Punarvasu, Puṣya, or Hasta, one should grind [the substance] together with one's own excrement and add one's own semen and blood to it; then, for whichever woman it is given, that woman becomes submissive. One should indeed recite this mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavati tripure*.
O Enchantress of the Three Worlds! Aiṃ drāṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauṃ! Bring [the person] named so-and-so quickly under my control, svāhā! Thus is the mantra.
Now, the ritual procedure for *guñjā* is written: having consecrated white *guñjā* at the time of twilight on a Saturday, one should then rise during the *brāhma-muhūrta* before the sun has risen.
Having become naked and using a peg made of *khadira* wood, one should uproot [the plant] along with its roots under the asterism of Puṣya or Hasta.

Together with a woman’s menstrual blood, one should apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*) consisting of *gorocanā*, *kāśmīra-kuṅkuma*, white sandalwood, and *rocanā*. Then, the woman, deluded by the arrows of Kāma, becomes overwhelmed. By means of this mantra:
One should recite the mantra: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus ends the Kāmabāṇa tilaka.
Now, the rites of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and so forth, as taught in other tantras, are written down:
having extracted the essence, something is also being told in brief regarding the subjugation and enchantment that generates delight for those possessed by desire. (3)
Therein, first is the procedure for the *tilaka*:
"A man who grinds together *lajjā*, *madhūka*, *kavya*, and the root of *nalini* with his own semen and applies it as a *tilaka*... (4)
From that very moment, it brings the three worlds under one's control;
this unsurpassed yoga was proclaimed by the sage Vātsyāyana. (5)
White mustard, the eight roots, mañjiṣṭhā, vacā, mustā, and kuṣṭha—
having combined these together, one should apply them to the forehead in the case of female genital blood-disorders.
He who applies this auspicious tilaka shall, in due course, bring the three worlds under his control;
being grateful, he shall make them subject to his will and rejoice for a long time upon this earth.
The wise person should take equal parts of Tagara, Pippalīmūla, Meṣīśṛṅgī, Kaṇā, and Jaṭā, and having combined these with their own five parts, bring them to a single state.
The man who applies a tilaka with honey on the day of the son of the Earth (Mangala-vāra) shall bring the entire world under his control; of this there is no doubt.
She who, having prepared yellow orpiment with her own menstrual blood,
should apply it as a tilaka on her forehead, will utterly delude her husband. (10)
Now, the procedure for collyrium:
On the day of the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī), the collyrium produced from soot fallen upon the head of a man in a cremation ground shall delude the entire world when applied as eye-salve.
Purifying rocanā, kesara, kanyā, and śilā, one should employ them all when they come within the range of vision; this will utterly delude [the enemy].
Having prepared a wick from *tālīśa*, *kuṣṭha*, and *nāgara*,
and having placed it in *siddhārtha* oil, one should apply the soot upon the head of a man.
One should apply this ointment; then, for all time in the three worlds, everyone who comes within the range of one's vision becomes like a servant. (14)
Śilā, kiñjalka, phalinī, rocanā, and likewise añjana—
when prepared under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, this is a supreme means of enchanting a couple.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, the procedure for the powder:
*kākajaṅghā*, realgar, the two wings of a bee, black lotus, and *tagara*—the powder of these, when cast, effects enchantment. (16)
This powder of the feathers of a *vātapaittika* crane and the excrement of a *mālāsava* crane, when thrown upon the head, causes delusion. (17)
Now, the procedure for consumption:
having extracted all the entrails and so forth from the belly of a wagtail (*khañjarīṭa*) and filling it with one's own semen, one should place it around the neck of a dog. (18)
Having formed the mudrā, the wise one should retain it in solitude for seven days;
afterwards, having extracted and purified it, he should form it into pills and dry them thoroughly.
This lamp-garland, offered according to the rules of consumption by the couple to one another, is proclaimed as the supreme observance that generates mutual affection. (20)
p.
31) Another opinion: Now I shall further proclaim another *tilaka* that fulfills all desires: *gorocana* and *vaṃśalocana*.

Having taken equal parts of fish gall, saffron from Kashmir, the filaments of *svayambhū* flowers, its own resin, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, red sandalwood, musk, camphor, and the roots of *kākajaṅghā*, one should grind them with water from a well, a pond, or a river, and [apply it] to the side of a young girl.

Having made a pill, one should prepare the pill in the shade. Having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead with that [pill], whichever woman one looks upon, she becomes submissive. With this mantra—*drauṃ vāṃ dhāṃ kṣauṃ aṃ kaṃ chaḥ*—one should [use] a stake made of buffalo bone measuring nineteen finger-breadths.
If one buries [the substance] consecrated one thousand times at the edge of a well in the name of someone, that person will be killed by a buffalo.

Oṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ ḷṃ [name] huṃ īṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ oṃ. With this mantra, one should empower a three-finger-long stake made of peacock bone a thousand times; then, by reciting the name of whomever one buries it at a crossroads, that person will wander there, remaining and roaming about that place.

Peace is attained by lifting [the object] for a mere moment. *Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ vrāṃ vrīṃ īṃ īṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ svāhā*. With this mantra, one should empower a stake made of sheep bone, twelve finger-breadths long, one thousand times; then, wherever one buries it in someone's house—
For him, every accomplishment remains unaccomplished.

O lady of excellent hips, one should meditate upon [the deity] resembling a bandhūka flower within the lamp of the mantra during the kumbhaka breath-retention; listen, for I shall describe its sixfold qualities.
Having meditated for one month, one will certainly bring a great woman;
by means of this mantra for one month, one may bring even a Naga maiden.
A celestial maiden [is attained] in three months at evening; it cannot be otherwise.
With this very mantra, "Oṃ haṃ haḥ," the wrathful sacrificers (krodhayājaka) are to be meditated upon. (23)

(32) For one who is to be sacrificed, [the path] resembling Rudra and held by the hand of Rudra leads to the world of humans in one month, and to the world of the Nāgas in two months, by means of the gods and demons. (24)
O Goddess of the Gods, in three months one reaches the heavenly world, without a doubt;
through the practice of yoga for six months, one makes the three worlds immovable.
Oṃ raktahaṭā raktagaṭā mukuṭadhāriṇī edhati svāhā. This king of mantras is the reverse piercing (ulṭā vedhā).
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ dhrīṃ vikṛtānanā bāhye phaṭ svāhā. Having written this mantra upon a yantra, if it is shown to someone, that person [is protected] from quotidian, tertian, and quartan fevers.

It is seized at that very moment and perishes; there is no doubt in this. *Oṃ bandhuna kṣayaṃ drīṃ drīṃ [name]'s self, by means of the eternal fever, at the mere binding of the leaf, throb! Svāhā!* This is the leaf for the purification of the eternal fever. *Oṃ kṣaḥ svāhā!* Water consecrated with this mantra—
Having thoroughly applied it to the feverish body, one should sprinkle [the patient] with that; by this, liberation from fever certainly occurs.
The divine instruction was delivered in due order to Siṃha, who had a donkey for a mount;
Vāyu, mounted upon a bear-horse, roared like a thundercloud. (26)
Having written this verse on a Sunday, one should place it upon the head;
by its mere placement, it shall remove a fever lasting for three months.
Then, having taken the blood of a wild cat and a wick made from lotus fibers, one should consecrate it seven times.
Then, one should cause soot to fall before Śiva using the oil produced from that;
with eyes anointed by it, one certainly becomes invisible. (29)

*Hebhir ihe bherihe*. Having taken water with this [mantra], having looked at it, and having recited it one thousand times, success is achieved within three nights by means of this very collyrium. One should cause soot to fall from a wick made of lotus fibers using oil; one whose eyes are anointed with that becomes invisible.
Then, having washed one's eyes with cow urine, one becomes visible once again.
Now, the mantra for subduing the ḍākinīs: Akṣaḥ, kṣāṃ, kṣaukājasinau;
the deity is Tattvadhūlinī; Ghonāśālinī; Bhamantri; Bandhuśanādaivataṃ; with Laghukaṇṭaka as the one who commands the people; the deity is Mahābhairava; the mandala is Acala.
(On Tuesday) Oṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ cchaḥ, homage to the kinsman of the Ḍākinīs!
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Vajra, the Lord Caṇḍeśvara; īṃ īṃ phaṭ svāhā!
This is the mantra for subduing all spirits and Ḍākinīs. Subduer, serpent, *laṅga*, elephant, *li*, *si*, *ma*, *ja*, bind at night!

"Immovable as a serpent-noose"—this is the mantra for subduing and binding. *Oṃ raṃ strīṃ śīghraṃ ha svāhā*. Having written [the name] of Tripurā upon a leaf of the *udanāla* plant with vermilion and powdered conch-shell, it should be purified;
within three days, she will come and meet with the fever. *Oṃ ahohaḥ [name of the woman]*.
"Bring [it] quickly, svāhā!"—thus is the summoning.

Oṃ strīṃ strīṃ valīṃ valīṃ īṃ ahaḥ phaṭ svāhā. One becomes healthy after bathing. "O Apsaraṇī, [make] so-and-so live! Having consecrated water seven times with this mantra, it should be given to the beloved woman for drinking. Oṃ namo jale mohe kule phalāni saṃkule svāhā.

If one gives [something] to someone after consecrating it seven times with this mantra, that person becomes submissive: *oṃ namo jale mohe drāṃ abjini phaṭ svāhā*. By means of this mantra, if one washes one’s face with water at dawn, one becomes beloved by all people and becomes a master of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā. Having consecrated betel leaf with this mantra, whoever it is to whom it is given shall become submissive.
Oṃ, salutation to Jale, to Mohe! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Grind, grind! Bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā!
Now, the practice for accomplishing the mantras of the yakṣiṇīs: Surasundarī, Manohāriṇī,
Kanakāvatī, Ratikarī, Kāmeśvarī, Naṭī, Anurāgiṇī, and Padminī— these eight yakṣiṇīs are the means for accomplishing one's desires.
34) Now, the sādhana of Surasundarī: Oṃ hrīṃ, come, come, O Surasundarī, svāhā!
Having gone to the abode of Vajrapāṇi and offered guggulu incense, one should worship her a thousand times at the three junctions of the day.
One should recite [the mantra] three times daily for the duration of a month; then, within that month, she becomes manifest.

On the final day, one should offer an *arghya* oblation with red sandalwood. Then, having arrived, she becomes a mother, a sister, or a wife, and performs exactly those tasks which are appropriate for them. If she becomes a mother, then...

She bestows perfected substances and elixirs. If she becomes a sister, then she gives priceless garments as before; if she becomes a wife, then she fulfills all prosperity. However, one must avoid sleeping with another woman here, for she is fond of sexual union, and otherwise she perishes.
Now, the sādhana for Manohāriṇī: Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha manohari svāhā.

Having gone to a confluence of rivers, having drawn a maṇḍala with sandalwood paste, and having offered incense of aguru, one should recite the mantra one thousand times every day for the duration of a month. Then, at the end of the month—
One should offer the *arghya* with sandalwood water and worship her with flowers and fruit with a single-pointed mind;
then, at the time of midnight, she certainly arrives. Having arrived, she carries out his command and gives a hundred gold pieces to that practitioner every day. || 2 ||

Now, the sādhana of Kanakāvatī: *oṃ hrīṃ kanakāvati maithunapriye āgaccha āgaccha svāhā*. Standing near a banyan tree (*vaṭavṛkṣa*), one should offer an oblation (*naivedya*) consisting of liquor, meat, and so forth to her with the root mantra, and having personally partaken of the remainder, [one should recite it] one thousand times.

One should recite the root mantra. One should perform this in this manner for up to seven days. On the eighth night, at the time of midnight, eight [women], adorned with garments and ornaments, [should be present].
Taking her retinue, she approaches; once arrived, she is to be desired and becomes his wife.
She provides clothing, ornaments, and food for twelve people, and she constantly grants eight *kalās* to the practitioner. || 3 ||
Now, the sādhana of Kāmeśvarī: *Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha kāmeśvari svāhā*.

Here, having drawn an image in the form of a woman upon a birch leaf with yellow pigment (gorocanā), and having worshipped it with either the sixteen or the five offerings (*upacāras*), one should then sit alone in a secluded place on a bed, with the mind fixed on her.
Having become [thus], one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times; then, at the end of the month, one should worship one's own wife with that same intention.

Then, having lit a lamp with honey and clarified butter every night and performed the ritual honors, one should recite the root mantra one thousand times. Thereafter, she will certainly arrive at the time of midnight.
However, other women are to be avoided. || 4 ||
Now, the sādhana for Ratipriyā: Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha ratikari svāhā.
Here, she should be painted on a cloth in her variegated form, adorned with garments and golden ornaments, holding a blue lotus in her hand, and appearing as a young maiden.
One should perform worship with jasmine flowers and offer incense of guggulu. Then, [one should recite the mantra] eight thousand times.
One should recite [the mantra] daily. At the end of the month, one should perform worship according to the rules. Incense and lamps should be lit;
then, at the time of midnight, she will certainly arrive. Once she has arrived, that woman should be loved with passion;
she becomes the practitioner's wife, protects his retinue, and provides divine, desirable food.
He gives. || 5 ||
Now, the practice for Padminī: *Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha padmini svāhā*.

Having drawn a maṇḍala with sandalwood paste in one's own home, one should cause her to be present there; having offered incense of guggulu, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times every day. Then, at the end of the month, on the night of the full moon—
Having performed the worship according to the rules, one should recite the mantra. At the end of the recitation, at the time of midnight, she invariably arrives; once arrived, she is to be enjoyed.
Having become his wife, she becomes the granter of all desires; she bestows upon the practitioner daily elixir, rejuvenation, and perfected substances. || 6 ||

Now, the *sādhana* of Naṭī: *Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha naṭi svāhā*. Having gone there beneath an *aśoka* tree, one should offer food such as fish and meat, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and a sacrificial oblation (*bali*), and recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day. Then, at the end of a month, she will certainly come; once arrived, she is like a mother or a sister.

Or she becomes his wife. If she is his mother, then she gives divine, desirable food, and she also gives garments, perfumes, and a hundred pieces of gold. If she is his sister, then she brings and gives him an excellent woman from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*. If she becomes his wife, then [she gives] the divine...
Within eight days, it bestows garments and an elixir.

Now, the sādhana for Anurāgiṇī: *oṃ hrīṃ anurāgiṇi āgaccha āgaccha svāhā*. Here, having drawn an image resembling a woman on birch bark with saffron from Kashmir, having performed the invocation and other rites, and having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, [one should offer] betel leaves.
Having offered [the oblation], one should recite the mantra a thousand times every day. One should recite it three times a day for one month;

at the end of the month, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to the rules and lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night. Then, at the time of dawn, she certainly arrives, and once she has arrived—
She grants all desires, bestows divine elixirs, and gives a thousand dīnāras every day; by her grace, one’s lifespan becomes a thousand years. || 8 ||
Now, the thirty-six yakṣiṇīs:
Vicitrā, Vibhramā, Haṃsī, Bhīṣaṇī, Janarañjinī, Viśālā, Madanā, Ghaṇṭā, Kālakarṇī, and Mahābhayā. (1)
Māhendrī, Śaṅkhinī, Cāndrī, Śmaśānā, Vaṭayakṣiṇī, Mekhalā, Vikalā, Lakṣmī, Mālinī, and Śatapatrikā. (2)
Sulocanā, Suśobhāḍhyā, Kapālinī, Viśālinī, Naṭī, Kāmeśvarī, Svarṇarekhā, and Surasundarī. (3)
Manoharā, Pramodānurāgiṇī, Nakhakeśikā, Bhāminī, Padminī, Svarṇavatī, and Ratipriyā. || 4 ||
These thirty-six yakṣiṇīs, who grant the desires for spiritual accomplishments,
have been described in detail by Mahādeva in the Karaṅkiṇīmata Tantra.
I shall describe in brief their great propitiation,
as well as the fruit they bestow when satisfied with one who is composed.
(1) Pure, one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times beneath a banyan tree;
thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice with campaka flowers mixed with honey and ghee.
The practitioner of mantra should perform [the rite] ten times over, just as it was declared by Śaṅkara;
then, O Goddess, she becomes perfected, wondrous, and the bestower of desired objects.
Oṃ vicitre citrarūpiṇi me siddhiṃ kuru 2 svāhā. This is the mantra.
(2) One should recite this mantra two hundred thousand times at night in a secluded cremation ground;
once ten percent of that amount has been offered as oblations with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, [the rite is complete]. || 9 ||
Vibhramā attains satisfaction with fifty men;
Śaṅkara said that she gives food and wealth every day. 10.
Oṃ hrīṃ, O Vibhramā, you whose form is the embodiment of enchantment, create enchantment! Rahi 2, O Blessed One, svāhā!
(3) Then, in a location within the city, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
when the fire sacrifice is performed with lotus petals mixed with ghee, it should be done according to the ten-part rule. || 11 ||
The female swan gives him collyrium by which he beholds the treasure hidden in the earth;
he recovers it with ease and is not overcome by obstacles.
Oṃ drīṃ namo haṃsi haṃsavāhini klīṃ klīṃ svāhā.
(4) Standing at the confluence of the three paths, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times, with a tenth part of that as the concluding oblation.
When offered as an oblation with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, Bhīṣaṇī grants whatever is desired.
Oṃ aiṃ drīṃ mahāmode bhīṣaṇi drāṃ drāṃ svāhā.

(5) Then, one should recite this mantra two hundred thousand times at night beneath a *kadamba* tree; thereafter, by performing a fire sacrifice with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, the Goddess becomes the bestower of good fortune. 14.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ janarañjini svāhā.
(6) Pure, one should repeat this mantra one hundred thousand times beneath a tamarind tree;
one should perform a fire sacrifice with lotus flowers accompanied by ghee. 15.
Then, O Goddess, she becomes perfected, traveling through the vast expanse of space;
and being pleased, she bestows upon the practitioner the divine elixir of mercury.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ viśāle strāṃstrīṃ ehyehi svāhā.
(7) One who is pure, standing at the king’s gate, should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times; then, having performed a fire sacrifice with ten parts of *mālatī* flowers mixed with milk. 17.
When Madanayakṣiṇī is pleased, she bestows a pill;
by keeping which in the mouth, a man becomes invisible, pure, and steadfast. (18)
Oṃ hrīṃ madane madanaviḍambini ālaye saṅgamaṃ dehi dehi śrīṃ svāhā.
(8) While sounding a fine bell, the practitioner should recite this mantra twenty thousand times.
Therein, the adept agitates the worlds by his mere sight. (19)
Oṃ aiṃ drīṃ, agitate the city, agitate the subjects, O Blessed One of deep resonance, O you who dwell in dreams, svāhā!
(9) Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, [one should perform the fire sacrifice] with fuel from the palāśa tree.
When an oblation is performed with offerings smeared with honey, Kālakarṇī becomes propitious.
When pleased, she indeed bestows happiness and becomes the cause of immobility;
the practitioner of mantra should constantly remember her, who performs various wonders.
(10) Oṃ hūṃ kālakarṇi ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! Wearing the bone-seal, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times in a cremation ground.
Then the Great Terrifying One, being propitiated, bestows upon him an elixir.
By merely consuming it, one may even cause mountains to tremble;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall not incur any disease.
Oṃ drīṃ mahābhaye preṃ svāhā.

(11) When the rainbow appears, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while standing amidst *nirguṇḍī* and *tulasī* plants; thereafter, it becomes perfected and bestows the siddhi of Pātāla. 24.
Oṃ hrīṃ māhendri mantrasiddhiṃ kuru kuru kulu 2 haṃsaḥ sohaṃ svāhā.
(12) The practitioner of mantra, being pure, should recite this mantra ten thousand times at sunrise;
thereafter, [he should perform the fire sacrifice] with a conch-shell rosary and fuel-sticks made of *karavīra* flowers. (25)
Then, being pure, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with ghee-eyed [seeds] in a tenth part [of the total];
thus the goddess Śaṅkhinī, the bestower of desires, will certainly become accomplished.
Oṃ hrīṃ śaṅkhadhāriṇi śaṅkhadhāraṇe drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ svāhā. (13) In this same manner, the sādhana of Cāndrī should also be understood.
(14) One who is pure should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times in a cremation ground.
The naked ascetic woman, being pleased, bestows collyrium in the cremation ground. || 27 ||
By that means, a man shall become invisible and may wander upon the surface of the earth;
he beholds and seizes treasure, and is not overcome by obstacles.
Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ, O dweller in the cremation ground, svāhā!

(15) Standing at the confluence of the three paths, seated beneath a banyan tree, one should indeed recite [the mantra] silently at night for three hundred thousand times; thereafter, the goddess Vaṭayakṣiṇī becomes accomplished. (29)
Being well-pleased, she bestows upon the practitioner divine garments and ornaments, the perfection of alchemy, elixirs, and divine collyrium.
(16) Oṃ śrīṃ drīṃ, O dweller of the banyan tree, born of the Yakṣa lineage, O Yakṣiṇī of the banyan tree, come, come! Svāhā!
[One should recite this] mantra at the foot of a Madhūka tree for a period of fourteen days.
If one recites the Mekhalā mantra, she, being pleased, bestows the most excellent collyrium.
Oṃ drīṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Madanamekhalā, the Deluder of Passion; svāhā.
(17) A man should mutter this mantra for three months while staying within a cave.
Then, O Goddess, she becomes perfected, free from defects, and the bestower of desired objects. 32.
Oṃ vikale aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ svāhā.

(18) Established in his own home, the practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times with red karavīra flowers, followed by a tenth part of that number [of oblations] using dūrvā grass and clarified butter. 32.
When performed at home, the yakṣiṇī named Lakṣmī becomes perfected;
she bestows divine elixirs, rejuvenators, and hidden treasures.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ lakṣmi kamaladhāriṇi haṃsaḥ sohaṃ svāhā.
(19) Standing at a crossroads during a time of calamity, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times;
Mālinī becomes perfected and bestows a divine sword. || 34 ||
By whose power one may obtain in this world a kingdom that is difficult to attain:
Oṃ drīṃ oṃ, obeisance to Mālinī! O beautiful woman, come, come; O Haṃsa-Haṃsī, unite me with my desired object, svāhā!
(20) That sage who recites a hundred thousand mantras in a forest of lotuses,
having attained perfection through oblations of milk and ghee, bestows the accomplishment of an earthly treasure.
Oṃ drīṃ śatapatrike drīṃ drīṃ śrīṃ svāhā. (21) Standing on a riverbank, the practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times;
when the fire-oblation of ghee has been performed with a tenth part of that number, the Goddess becomes pleased. || 36 ||
He gives him a pair of sandals in the sky according to his desire;
with the speed of mind and wind, the practitioner goes and returns. (37)
Oṃ drīṃ klīṃ sulocane, grant me success, grant me success, svāhā!
(22) Wearing red garments, the practitioner should recite this for fourteen days; then the goddess Śobhanā, the bestower of enjoyments, will become perfected. 38.
Oṃ drīṃ, O beautiful one with the sprouts of the Aśoka tree in the palm of your hand, śrīṃ kṣaḥ svāhā!
The practitioner who observes the great vow, by eating meals of śāli rice, should recite this mantra two hundred thousand times; that sage shall obtain a skull-cup. (39)
It bestows upon the practitioner the power of traveling through space, union with dream-forms from afar, seeing from a distance, and so forth. (40)
Oṃ aiṃ kapālini drāṃ drīṃ klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ klaiṃ klauṃ klaḥ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ sakalahrīṃ phaṭ svāhā.
(24) The preceptor should recite this mantra fifty thousand times on the bank of a river.
When oblations are offered with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, the Goddess becomes the bestower of good fortune.

as well as the flowers and leaves of palāśa, the leaves of ambara and bilva, aśvagandhā and other fragrant substances— all these, according to the specific requirements of the treatment, one should use to rub the body with an ointment.
Furthermore, he who, having cast a water-pot [over the image], performs the ritual bath, always obtains a woman, ointment for the body, and clothing. (Śirolepana, p. 55)
Having discarded the wearing of another's clothes, she should perform [the rite]. Seated upon a *bhadra* seat...
she should cast it into the water; that woman who draws out the machine situated within the jar from among the women, she should then worship as the woman facing her.
With garments, ornaments, vermilion, fragrant flowers, and other such items, one should cause the worship of the Lord to be performed in the home; one should worship Śiva together with the Goddess.
That man should give a sacrificial fee consisting of a white cow together with her calf;
now I shall describe the fruit of the bath as it was spoken by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains wealth;
one desiring peace attains peace; and the unfortunate becomes fortunate.
Likewise, a king who has been deprived of his kingdom will certainly regain his kingdom;
one without a wife shall obtain a wife, and one seeking happiness shall attain happiness.

Thus ends the fruit of bathing for women and men. *Huṃ amukaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having gone to a cremation ground, one should very quickly take the breast-milk of an owl, a pigeon, and a *kāñjīra* bird, and recite [this mantra] for seven days.

"Oṃ amukaṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Reciting this mantra ten thousand times while standing near a *bhānu* tree, one should then perform a fire sacrifice (*havana*) with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) in a tenth part of that number; this brings about the power of causing someone to fall down.
Having first recited the mantra "Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ" ten thousand times, if one recites it during a time of drought,

a great rain will fall. Having first recited the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Varade Svāhā" ten thousand times, one should perform a fire sacrifice (havana) with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood using a tenth part of that number.

One should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*); then one will obtain the fruit for all time. *Huṃ huṃ huṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ amukaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*), and having smeared fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood with blood, one should offer them as a tenth part (*daśāṃśa*) of that number; by means of a single thousand [offerings] performed under the name of whomever [the target], he [is subdued].

One is seized by the Mahendra-jvara; its pacification occurs through ten thousand oblations. With this very mantra, one should offer ten thousand fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). Then—
The Rākṣasas, beginning with Vibhīṣaṇa, become granters of boons. Oṃ hūṃ vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaṃ vaḥ oṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra for seizing fever.

Oṃ aiṃ kṣili kili phaṭ svāhā. Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times over udumbara wood mixed with the three sweets (trimadhu), one should perform one thousand oblations; this brings about a great rain during a time of drought. Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ draiṃ drauṃ haḥ oṃ svāhā. This mantra...

Having first recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should offer oblations of *bilva* wood-samids mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). Thereupon, all the people of the realm become one's servants. *Oṃ drīṃ oṃ drīṃ huṃ oṃ svāhā*.
Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times, one should offer oblations of *darbha* wood-samids mixed with ghee and milk, numbering one-tenth of that [recitation].
From one hundred thousand oblations, there is the pacification of all diseases.

Oṃ klīṃ [Name] khe khe svāhā. One should first offer this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*) as an oblation (*juhuyāt*). Then, one should offer a tenth part of that number—namely one thousand—of *nyagrodha* wood fuel sticks mixed with honey. By performing this many oblations, the wife of a great king comes under one's control; what need is there to mention the women of other worlds? Oṃ drīṃ Gomukhi.

"O Gomukhī, O you who possess a thousand sons, come to this ground of flesh from the terrifying serpent's coils; svāhā! With this mantra, one desiring subjugation should offer red karavīra flowers mixed with honey; one should offer salt to attract a woman;
one desiring love should offer the aforementioned mixture; and one should offer vermilion to cause the agitation of a city.

If one performs an offering of husks and the tips of ears of grain, it becomes a rite of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*); if one performs an offering of human flesh mixed with clarified butter, one shall become a great lord of wealth.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! With this mantra, one should offer oblations of ghee combined with *śrīphala* fruits. By a hundred oblations, wisdom is attained;
by a thousand, the acquisition of cattle occurs; by a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), the acquisition of a thousand villages occurs; and by one hundred and twenty-five thousand (*sapādalakṣa*).
The king regains his lost kingdom.
Oṃ aiṃ drīṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. With this mantra, one should offer a thousand oblations of crow-flesh and cock-seed with pungent oil, while reciting the name ending in the syllable *drīṃ*.
If one recites [the mantra] using the name of someone, that person becomes insane; by performing a *homa* with a thousand grains of rice, they become restored to health.
*Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ kṣaṃ klīṃ svāhā*. Recitation should be performed with this mantra:
by reciting it seven times, purification of the body occurs; by reciting it a hundred times, the fruit of bathing at all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) is obtained.
With one thousand [recitations], there is an increase of intelligence; with ten thousand, one becomes a great poet who composes thousands of verses;
with one hundred thousand, one becomes a possessor of a retentive memory (śrutidhara); with two hundred thousand, one becomes a knower of all the scriptures;
with three hundred thousand, one becomes a knower of the past, future, and present; and with four hundred thousand, one becomes a lord of the planets.
By five hundred thousand recitations, one becomes a knower of the specific details of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis;

by six hundred thousand, one becomes a Vajra-tantra practitioner; by seven hundred thousand, one dries up rivers and attains friendship with Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others; otherwise, if one performs the recitation according to the method taught in the Vajra [Tantra], then this person is consecrated by the Seer.

He becomes equal to a hundred great sages; he becomes free from distress when multiplied by a thousand; furthermore, he becomes a disturber of cities when multiplied by ten thousand; with six times that, he agitates the three worlds;
with the third [multiple], he agitates the seven netherworlds; and with the fourth, he agitates heaven.
With the fifth [mudrā], one agitates the seven worlds situated above; with the sixth, one agitates the three worlds;

with the seventh, one agitates all living beings, such as bipeds and quadrupeds; with the eighth, one attracts both the stationary and the moving; and with the ninth, one [acts] oneself throughout all the worlds.

With ten lakhs [of recitations], one’s movement becomes covered by the mouth of Nārada; one becomes capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise. Furthermore, if a person should recite even once according to the rite of casting nectar (*amṛta-kṣepaṇa*), they should offer an oblation of white *karavīra* flowers mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*); such a person becomes beloved by all people.

One should offer *aśoka* flowers with ghee; one becomes free from sorrow. One who desires to regain a lost kingdom should perform a *homā* of *śrīphala* fruits; he regains his lost kingdom. One desiring to cause a downfall should offer lotus flowers mixed with clarified butter, or alternatively, *kumudinī* flowers.
If one offers peacock flesh mixed with pungent oil while reciting the *kūṭa* [mantra], death occurs. If one offers betel nut,
pungent oil, and iron powder, eruptions break out over the entire body.

Through the oblation of *kṣīri* leaves and *bilva* leaves, pacification (*śānti*) occurs. One should offer sesame fuel-sticks with pungent oil; by that, inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) occurs. When the powder of *dhattūra*, the powder of bone, and iron powder with pungent oil are offered, the destruction of enemies occurs quickly. One should offer "great flesh" (*mahāmāṃsa*) with clarified butter for one's heart's desire.
Everything comes to pass.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Treasury of Mantras," in the Uḍḍāmareśvara Mahātantra, extracted from the Vīrabhadreśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Devī. || 13 ||

Now begins the fourteenth chapter. *Klīṃ*, O you who are afflicted by desire, O Kāmamekhalā, O you who possess sense-objects, O you who grant excellent pleasure, O Blessed One, bring [the person named] so-and-so under my control!

*Kuru vaśaṃ kuru klīṃ namaḥ svāhā*. At the time of eating, one should consume seven morsels of food consecrated seven times with this mantra. On the seventh day, whether it be a woman or a man, they become submissive and offer themselves.

Oṃ hūṃ svāhā. One should recite this mantra at the three junctions of the day; the destruction of enemies will occur. Klīṃ kālikāli mahākāli kole kinyā svāhā. Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (ayuta), one should perform one thousand fire-oblations (homa) at the time of twilight; thereafter, Kaṅkālī becomes a granter of boons.
He gives four pieces of gold every day.

Oṃ drīṃ drīṃ drūṃ draiṃ drauṃ draḥ huṃ namaḥ svāhā. Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (ayuta), one should offer only clarified butter (ājya) into the fire; from this, attraction (ākarṣaṇa) occurs.
Oṃ drauṃ drauṃ drīṃ drīṃ huṃ namaḥ svāhā. By reciting this mantra according to the previously mentioned procedure for half a month, summoning occurs. Oṃ hūṃ oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hīṃ svāhā. Thus.
The first section on the classification of swords. The mantra for reviving all [the dead]:
*oṃ huṃ drīṃ draṃ drauṃ draḥ huṃ huṃ*. By this mantra, there is the destruction of all fevers. *Dīṃ haṃsini svāhā*. By this mantra, there is the subjugation of all people. *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ hrīṃ phaṭ*.

Svāhā! One should recite this mantra ten thousand times while employing the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), seated upon a corpse-throne, and one must not reveal the heart-mantra. Having seized such-and-such a woman [and] having made it into a pill, by placing it in the mouth, one becomes a Vidyādhara. Oṃ.

*Hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ*. One should recite this mantra according to the previously mentioned procedure; the accomplishment of the *pādukā* (magical sandals) will occur. *Oṃ kṣaṃ kṣaṃ hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. One should recite this mantra in the previous sequence;
the accomplishment of the *vetāla* (vampire/demon) will occur. *Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*. By means of this mantra, [one should employ] a human skull (*narakapāla*).

Having taken it, one should place human oil in it and light a wick that increases the vision of crows; on a Saturday during the new moon of the dark fortnight, one should cause soot to fall in a blind well,
a cremation ground, or an empty temple, while reciting the previously mentioned mantra for that duration of time.
For as long as it takes for the remainder of the wick to burn, at the conclusion a profuse offering (bali) must be made; there,
taking the sacrificial pillar and with eyes anointed by that perfected ointment (siddhāñjana), one is not seen even by gods or demons, let alone by other people.

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ hrīṃ hrīṃ—this is the Śaṅkhinī-vidyā. Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ—this is the Puṣpāñjali-vedha. Huṃ huṃ—this is the Huṃkāra-vedha. Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ—this is the Ālaya-vedha. Hrāṃ is the mantra for the Śivā-vedha. Hrīṃ—thus [it is].
The piercing through the collision of the *bhramarāvarta* [mudrā]. *Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ chaḥ chaḥ svāhā*.
Having fashioned an iron trident and having ground poison with blood, one should smear that [poison] upon the trident and consecrate it ten thousand times.
Having performed [this rite], if one buries it in the earth under the name of someone, that person's death occurs swiftly.

Oṃ hrīṃkāri hūṃkāri kapāli, pierce the male, the female, and the neuter; O you of great repose, O granter of fearlessness, O you named Immortal, act, act! Destroy the fever! From the clamor of abuse, draw forth the supreme power, she who is joined with all powers! For the rite of pacification: huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Whoever mentally recollects this great vidyā that brings enemies under control becomes fearless everywhere.

Oṃ oṃ oṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ. Having recited this mantra, it becomes a destroyer of poisons, both stationary and mobile. Oṃ asthi yasthiṃ vidrānidrā sannividyā rā ṭaṃ ṭīṃ drīṃ samāsaṃ maṭaṃṭīṃ chaṃ chaṃ. By this [mantra]...
One should offer a thousand burnt oblations of crow feathers with the mantra while uttering the name of the person; that person is then expelled.
O woman! When ten thousand recitations have been performed with this mantra, the science of poetry arises.
Indeed, one should recite the *strīmaṇiśakunavidyā*; it instantly produces poetic talent. *Haṃ aiṃ haṃ haṃ aiṃ vada vada vāgvādini svāhā*.

Having recited this mantra seven times, it produces increasingly greater poetic skill. *Oṃ haṃ chaṃ chaṃ chaṃ aiṃ namaḥ svāhā*. From a thousand recitations, this mantra grants ever-increasing poetic inspiration.

Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ [jaṃ]—this instantly paralyzes the speech of the speaker from the moment it is seen. Huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ khaṃ khaṃ khaṃ khaṃ chaṃ chaṃ: this is the vidyā that paralyzes speech and restores life to the vital breath. Drīṃ: piercing by sight, piercing beyond the range of sight. Hrīṃ.

The mantra for piercing all: *draṃ drauṃ drauṃ drauṃ draṃ amukaṃ bhejibheji hrīṃ chaṃ chaṃ chaṃ*. This "Reviver of Explosions" (*visphoṭakasaṃjīvinī*), through its mere observation, brings about the accomplishment of one's purpose. *Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ*, destroy the Rākṣasas of the east; shatter all [obstacles]; satisfy [them] and delude them with a great sound!
*Huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā* (p.
61) is the mantra for slaying all *bhūtas*. *Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ drāṃ chaḥ chaḥ chaḥ*.

This vidyā, which brings about all pacification through the fire-oblation (*homa*) of *dūrvā* grass and milk, is as follows: *huṃ pañcāṇḍaṃ cāṇḍaṃ drīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. By means of this mantra, one should empower a human-bone stake seven finger-breadths long one thousand times; whoever has it buried in their house, for that person there shall be the destruction of their fortress.

When it has been extracted, health is restored. With this mantra—*huṃ kṣaṃ amukaṃ phaṭ svāhā*—one should offer the flesh of the *pecaka* bird mixed with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) into the fire. By performing one thousand oblations, one brings down the enemy. *Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dhuṃ dhuṃ haṃ haḥ svāhā*.

This is indeed the vidyā named Trailokyavijayā. One should remember this mantra mentally; it bestows all desires: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ viśvarūpiṇi piśācini bhūtabhaviṣyādikaṃ vada vada me karṇe kathaya kathaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra...
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times at the three junctions of the day.
Every day, one should offer purified water along with ghee and a ball of rice on top of a palace at night;
then whatever news there is in the three worlds, whether past or future, will come to the ear of the practitioner.
He says:
oṃ raṃ rāṃ saṃ sāṃ laṃ lāṃ haṃ haḥ saṃsaḥ khaṃkhaḥ taṃtaḥ dhaṃsaṃ sphuṃ sphaḥ hrīṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ kṣauṃ sauṃ saḥ chaṃ chaḥ dhaṃsaḥ sphuṃ sphaḥ hrīṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ kṣauṃ saṃ phaṃ phaḥ

*Huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra for destroying all poisons. *Sacārācare oṃ sacārācare oṃ huṃ huṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ kṣakṣakṣaḥ hasaḥ oṃ saṃ huṃ hrīṃ*, by the power of Viṣṇu, the lord of all, and by the pride of Śaṅkara, with the speed of the wind.
By the splendor of the sun and the radiance of the moon, [I declare] enmity, arrows, and chaff; speak all that removes poison!

Destroy, destroy all *rākṣasas*! Shatter, shatter all the wicked! Delude, delude, O God! *Huṃ phaṭ svāhā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā!* Having recited this mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times—
On the seventh day (p. 62), success in summoning occurs.

Oṃ hrīṃ [Name] chaḥ chaḥ. With this mantra, a stake made of human bone eleven finger-breadths long is consecrated one thousand times; if one buries it in someone’s house, that person’s fortress and their very existence are destroyed, but once it is extracted, they regain their health.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Kāla, Kaṅkāla, Mahākāla, you of the terrifying countenance! Seize so-and-so! Pierce him with the trident!
Cut him with the sword! Huṃ phaṭ chaḥ chaḥ svāhā!
With this mantra, a twenty-one-finger-long stake made of Vibhītaka wood is empowered one thousand times; [it is used] for whomsoever...

If it is buried at the door of a house, the immediate downfall of that person's body occurs. *Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ huṃ [Name] chaḥ chaḥ*. With this mantra, a nine-finger-long stake made of *siddhikāṣṭha* wood, consecrated one thousand times, is buried in whose house; he becomes submissive.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mātaṅgini aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ svāhā. By means of this mantra, if one performs one thousand burnt offerings (homa) of black mustard seeds mixed with salt and ghee while uttering the name of a person, one brings that woman or man under control and effects their attraction.

Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ chaḥ chaḥ! With this mantra, one should empower a stake made of *vāḍava* wood, thirteen finger-breadths in length, by reciting it a thousand times; whoever has it buried in their house becomes blind in both eyes.

Oṃ chaḥ oṃ chaḥ chaḥ. With this mantra, one should empower a ten-finger-long stake made of *bilva* wood a thousand times; whoever has it buried in their house, they, along with their retinue, shall become a *preta*. Oṃ hrīṃ [Name], give her to me, svāhā. With this mantra...
One should consecrate a five-finger-long wooden stake made of *pāṭala* wood one thousand times with a mantra;
by burying it in a temple under the name of a person, that person quickly obtains a maiden.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Exposition of the Treasury of Mantras, in the Great Tantra of Uḍḍāmareśvara, extracted from the Vīrabhadreśvara Tantra as proclaimed by the illustrious Śiva. || 14 ||
(p. 63) Now begins the fifteenth chapter.

Having drawn a six-cornered yantra, one should write the mantra "Oṃ Kurukulle svāhā" in the eastern corner of that six-cornered figure. One should write the two syllables "Kuru" in another corner. Each syllable should be written in a clockwise sequence. Then, having written this mantra on a birch-bark leaf (bhūrjapatra),...
When placed on one part of the threshold at the door of a house, it expels the house-snake; when placed at the entrance of a burrow, that which dwells within the burrow surely perishes.
A red *karavīra* flower smeared with the ashes of mango leaves becomes white at that very moment.

Likewise, by means of processed sulphur fumes, even mother-of-pearl becomes [flame-colored]. In the world, the flower of the red oleander known as *hayamāra*, when combined with sulphur and a cotton wick, ignites at that very moment. Similarly, when a coating is applied with *ṭaṅkana* and turmeric, it acquires the luster of saffron.

When dried old cow-dung is cast into water, then, due to its intense heat, bubbles arise from it. In this same way, when the white [substance] touches the surface of the earth upon the ground, the red karavīra tree is produced. One should place it into the copper vessel, like a bee into a jar.
A slight passion of the mind arises through the dye of betel, yet it perishes like the dye of turmeric from the rays of the sun.
Oṃ hūṃ! It is destroyed by the cry of the *kururu* bird (commonly known as the *kurala* or saffron-colored partridge).
Its name is also *kroñca*; having shown the tongue marked with *krīṃ* and the smear adhering to the center of the palm of the left hand,
one should again show it from the palm as it is smeared with the ashes of the risen *viśvadhārā*.

O you of wondrous intellect, having purified the milk of cows and other animals by means of the milk of a child, and having placed it warm in a bronze vessel, one should maintain it with great intensity; by the addition of rice, it becomes milk.
Having ignited a pouch made of birch bark with sesame oil, one should prepare various kinds of food and delicacies, as follows:

It is prepared in an iron vessel. Having wrapped a pala of vārtākarañjikā with a thread and ignited it, one should set it ablaze; when wrapped with that thread, the thread burns away while the vārtāka is cooked.
Having written the seven vowels in the first row, and having written the seven consonant groups beginning with *ka* in the row below that,

one should write [the remaining elements] in the row below that in the sequence beginning with turmeric (*haridrā*). Therein, through the conjunction of vowels and consonants, by means of contraction and contact with the squares of the syllables and so forth, it arises among many in the midst.
A thief who has received a signal and made a secret agreement knows even his own vision regarding the seven notes and so forth.
How could a thief, who delights in the moment amidst his activities, be recognized by noble wealth?
Having cast a *dhattūra* seed anywhere, he then eats it; from that, the fruit of its qualities and so forth is obtained.
"He is that thief. However, thieves who move about only slightly will reveal themselves upon obtaining the object.

Furthermore, the syllables of a thief's name written with the milky sap of trees such as the *kṣīrī* or *arka*, whether inscribed on the palm of the hand or subsequently made upon birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*), can be detected by touching them during a massage; thereafter, they may be consumed.

One gives an unscratched piece of earth from the interior of an enemy's house, accompanied by a leaf inscribed with the thief's name. Likewise, earth from water, accompanied by a leaf inscribed with the name of a good person, sinks in water; having touched it, one declares, "This man is the thief."
When minute lines drawn with milk or water are rubbed with charcoal powder, they become clear.

Even a counterfeit letter written in reverse becomes a distinct reflection in a mirror or similar surface; due to the reversal of the letters, the arrangement is magnified, and the ink becomes exceedingly firm.
65) In a vessel of equal copper, rubbed for one *yāma* with *nimba* and *tālaka*, let the procedure be as follows, with equal parts: *āmalakī*, *harītakī*, [and] *bibhītaka*.
By means of rubbing with all the ingredients including *rasaka* and *kāñjala*, in such a manner that each substance individually becomes a paste (*masi*) within a single watch (*yāma*),
the powder of the bark of the *śirīṣa* tree— excluding *khadira*— produces the red color of betel (*tāmbūlarāga*). Tiryak...

On the ground, a coconut fruit together with its kernel is split in two by a single blow from the mouth [of a statue] at the pericarp; or, without shoes made of light wood and fine craftsmanship, one foot wanders about;
or, having applied a foot smeared with the kernel of a *guñjā* seed and rendered rigid, one reaches the very tip of the forefoot.
Then it revolves; attached to the bottom of the foot, it rises up.
In this way, a balance made of light wood, with its mouth-cloth provided for the purpose of mocking the city of sin, is placed by him upon the waist over white cloth and so forth.
The fire remains present, abiding within the rising [substance]; thus,
even when the Jambu tree and others are covered by dense cloth, it does not burn charcoal placed in an inverted bronze vessel,
yet it does burn cloth, even when mixed with cold water.
A flask infused with the powder of *ānata* fruit becomes sharp; and when placed in a bronze vessel, that which was heavy and incapable of being lifted no longer remains so, but instead turns bitter.
Furthermore, that which was sour becomes sweet through the application of collyrium (*kajjala*) and the powder of *cavikā*, even in the case of a book whose pages have been inscribed in sequence.

It is cooked according to one's desire: for instance, when fire is ignited with honey in a more pleasant cauldron, or when [the vessel] is turned upside down in a pit filled with water; it spontaneously emits bright flames and spews forth smoke by itself, provided two wicks are inserted whose cores are filled with rabbit dung.
Even when the tortoises are positioned below as excrement,
this application should be performed upon the tube and other vessels with a sharp-tipped ember of burning smoke, which acts like a wick ignited by blazing flames above, within the *vālivāta* wind.
p.

66) Even the mark of a thread, hidden as far as the fingers of the left hand, appears as no mark at all when observed by a person with uneven or even syllables; one should know that such a person is unequal [in fortune]. [This is taught] in the *Pañcadāḍima*.
One should know that there will be as many pills as there are [units] multiplied by the peak. When there is an untimely curvature,
then, having mixed it with the powder of *mathaphala* and with ash, *kākañjikā* suddenly arises together with ghee.
In water that is unfathomable and still, one may write thoughts and the like with powdered incense; though it speaks as if afraid, it does not sink.
One who has been possessed by the spirit of the *samadaśa* [demon] remains holding a pestle, even while immersed in ghee.
Under the Puṣya asterism, even a child can hit a distant target with an arrow whirled around with saffron.
It is pierced. A heap of cow dung is seen burnt in the middle by the light of a wick-lamp, appearing like the blood of a slain hare; even there, there is some oil.
When a cotton wick the size of a mustard seed is combined with oil from a white *arka* fruit and placed in the flame of a lamp, [it burns].
